source_text: Certe in his locis Apostolum de peccato naturali disseruisse contendis. Ad hoc supra dixerat usque ad legem fuisse, ut intellegeretur post legem esse desisse; nunc autem de eodem dicit, quod coeperit crescere et abundare post legem. Catholico intellectui, quem sequimur, utrumque hoc convenire monstravimus; tuo vero dogmati qua impudentia vindicatur, ut unum idemque peccatum lege lata superius quidem defecisse, nunc autem crevisse dicatur? Quomodo ergo post legem abundavit naturale peccatum? Acriusne coeperunt genitalia commoveri, ut de augmentis et novitate motuum peccato tuo virtus videatur adiuncta? An lex data nascentibus est, ut qui de libidine, quam dicis diabolicam esse et radicem fructumque peccati, geniti erant, admonerentur emendare quod facti erant, et gestum corrigere quem habuerant, cum eos generarent parentes? Cogerent postremo, quae facta erant, infecta esse, quod illi audire videlicet renuentes inoboedientiae crimen incurrerent? At hoc a nullo stultorum, nedum a lege, quam Deus dedit, poterat imputari.
pass_a_gloss: Certainly in these places you contend that the Apostle discussed a natural sin. Toward this he had said above that it was until the law, so that it would be understood to have ceased after the law; but now about the same he says that it began to grow and abound after the law. We have shown that both of these fit the catholic understanding which we follow; but with what shamelessness is it vindicated for your dogma, that one and the same sin with the law passed is said above indeed to have failed, but now to have grown? How therefore after the law did a natural sin abound? Did the genitals begin to be moved more sharply, so that from increments and a newness of motions a virtue seem joined to your sin? Or was a law given to those being born, so that those who had been begotten from lust, which you say is diabolical and a root and fruit of sin, would be warned to amend what they had been made, and to correct the gesture which they had had when the parents generated them? Finally would they force those things which had been done to be undone, which they, namely refusing to hear, would incur a crime of disobedience? But this could be imputed by none of the foolish, much less by a law which God gave.

lemmas.lexica: LS libido; Blaise not a nature-sin substance
LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin

pass_b_english: You certainly contend that in these passages the apostle discussed natural sin. Earlier, he said it existed until the law, so that we would understand it ceased after the law. Now, however, he says of the same sin that it began to grow and abound after the law. We have shown that both statements fit the catholic understanding we follow. But with what shamelessness are they claimed for your doctrine, so that one and the same sin is said earlier to have ceased when the law was given, and now to have grown? How, then, did natural sin abound after the law? Did the genitals begin to move more fiercely, so that increased and novel movements seem to have added power to your sin? Or was a law given to newborn children, admonishing those begotten from sexual desire—which you call diabolical and the root and fruit of sin—to amend what they had been made, and correct the activity they had undergone when their parents begot them? Were they finally to compel what had happened not to have happened, and by refusing to hear this incur the crime of disobedience? No fool, much less the law God gave, could charge them with that (compare Romans 5:13; Romans 5:20) (Romans 5:13) (Romans 5:20) (Romans 5:13; Romans 5:20).

choices.why: Julian refuses to make marital desire a nature-sin substance planted by the devil.
Parents insofar as parents are not guilty; keep the forensic 'in quantum parentes sunt'.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.
